title: Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having personally abandoned discontent and aroused satisfaction, on that occasion recited this verse: I abandon pleasure and displeasure, All household thoughts,…
content:
Then the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, having personally abandoned discontent and aroused satisfaction, on that occasion recited this verse:

I abandon pleasure and displeasure,
All household thoughts,
Making no place anywhere
That could become a basis for sensual desire.
One who has escaped the forest of greed,
Escaped all sensual desire,
Free from greed, not clinging —
He is truly called a monk.
Whatever earth element, space element,
All the form realm in the world —
All things are subject to change,
All things are impermanent.
Whoever understands this,
His conduct is true.
Beings are always attached
To various attachments —
To what they see, hear,
Smell, taste, touch.
Whoever abandons desire here,
With mind undefiled,
Not clinging here or there —
He is called a sage (muni).
Concerning the sixty views
Belonging to wrong thoughts —
Worldlings cling to them,
Grasp and cling.
The monk who has no defilements,
Speaks no evil words,
Clear-minded, always concentrated,
Without deceit, careful —
Escaped from all craving.
The sage who has attained
The peaceful state of Nibbāna,
Awaiting the time of his end,
With mind perfectly still,
Serenely passes into Nibbāna.

title: “He who dwells attending to the beautiful, Unrestrained in the senses, Immoderate in food, Lazy, inactive — Māra overthrows him As wind a weak tree.”…
content:
“He who dwells attending to the beautiful,
Unrestrained in the senses,
Immoderate in food,
Lazy, inactive —
Māra overthrows him
As wind a weak tree.”

“He who dwells contemplating the foul,
Well-restrained in the senses,
Moderate in food,
Faithful, energetic —
Māra does not overthrow him,
As wind a rocky mountain.”

title: Sensual desires are many, sweet, and agreeable, Disquieting the mind in many ways. Seeing the danger in these strands of pleasure, I went forth, great…
content:
Sensual desires are many, sweet, and agreeable,
Disquieting the mind in many ways.
Seeing the danger in these strands of pleasure,
I went forth, great king!
Like fruits falling from a tree,
Both young and old, when the body breaks,
Seeing this, I went forth,
The ascetic life is supreme,
Great king!

title: “Through many a birth in samsara I have wandered, Seeking but not finding the builder of this house. Suffering is birth again and again.” “O…
content:
“Through many a birth in samsara I have wandered,
Seeking but not finding the builder of this house.
Suffering is birth again and again.”

“O house-builder, you are seen!
You shall not build a house again.
All your rafters are broken,
Your ridge-pole is shattered.
My mind has attained the unconditioned,
And the extinction of craving has been reached.”

title: “Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent,…
content: “Form, monks, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of form — that too is impermanent. Form that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Feeling, monks, is impermanent … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition for the arising of consciousness — that too is impermanent. Consciousness that has arisen from the impermanent, monks, how could it be permanent? Seeing thus, monks, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with form … disenchanted with feeling … disenchanted with perception … disenchanted with formations … disenchanted with consciousness. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate … He knows: ‘… there is no more of this state of being.’”

title: “Cunda, I do not teach merely for the sake of preventing defilements in the present life. Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for…
content: “Cunda, I do not teach merely for the sake of preventing defilements in the present life. Cunda, I do not teach the Dhamma only for the sake of eradicating defilements in the future. Cunda, I teach the Dhamma both for preventing defilements in the present life and for eradicating defilements in the future.”

title: “Monks, there are these five defilements of the mind because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not…
content: “Monks, there are these five defilements of the mind because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. What five? Sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt. These five defilements of the mind, monks, because of which the mind becomes defiled, not malleable, not wieldy, not radiant, brittle, and not properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements.”

title: Elder Nun Abhirūpa Nandā: Nandā, look at this body — A collection of many diseases, impure, Full of stench, rotting. Develop your mind, Contemplate the…
content:
Elder Nun Abhirūpa Nandā:

Nandā, look at this body —
A collection of many diseases, impure,
Full of stench, rotting.
Develop your mind,
Contemplate the nature of foulness,
Achieve one-pointedness,
With mind well concentrated.

Practice the signless,
Abandon the underlying tendency to conceit.
By fully understanding conceit,
You will live at peace.

title: “And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful,…
content: “And how, monks, is a monk called a ‘noble one’? He has made distant evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, fearful, producing painful results, leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, monks, a monk is called a noble one.”

title: “Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw beings with little dust in their…
content: “Monks, the Blessed One Vipassī, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye and saw beings with little dust in their eyes and with much dust in their eyes, with sharp faculties and with dull faculties, with good dispositions and with bad dispositions, some easy to teach and some hard to teach, and a few who saw the danger in rebirth in another world and the danger of faulty actions. Just as in a blue lotus pond, a red lotus pond, or a white lotus pond, some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, do not rise above the water, and are nourished underwater; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, and reach the water’s surface; some blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses are born in the water, grow in the water, rise up above the water and are not wetted by the water.”
